The pie charts compares the age groups of the population in two countries, Country A and Country B, in 2020.

In Country A, children aged 0 to 14 were the biggest group with 41%. People from 15 to 29 was 28% and 30 to 44 was 16%. The older groups were small, 45 to 64 was 11% and the people over 65 was only 4%.

Country B was very different. The biggest group was 45 to 64 years with 28% and the over 65 was 24%, which is much higher than in Country A. The group of 30 to 44 had 19%, and 15 to 29 had 16%. The children was the smallest group with only 13%.

Overall, it is clear that Country A has a very young population because most of people are young, but Country B has an older population. In Country A the percentage go down when the age go up, but in Country B it is opposite.
samples.why: Relevant comparison with accurate figures · overview present but late and repetitive · mechanical organisation and linking · limited range of vocabulary · several agreement and article errors which do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The pie charts compare the age profiles of the populations of Country A and Country B in 2020.

Overall, Country A had a very young population, with the proportion of people in each age group declining steadily as age increased. Country B, on the other hand, had a much older population, with its largest share in the 45–64 bracket.

In Country A, children aged 0–14 made up the largest group, at 41%, and people aged 15–29 accounted for a further 28%. This means that more than two-thirds of the population were under 30. The share then fell to 16% for those aged 30–44 and 11% for the 45–64 group, while only 4% of people were aged 65 or over.

The situation in Country B was almost the reverse. The 45–64 age group was the largest, at 28%, followed closely by the over-65s, who represented nearly a quarter of the population (24%). The middle age group, 30–44, made up 19%, whereas young people aged 15–29 and children accounted for just 16% and 13% respectively. Therefore, the proportion of elderly people in Country B was six times higher than in Country A.
samples.why: Clear overview of the contrasting patterns · key features highlighted with accurate figures and a valid comparison · clear paragraphing · range of linkers with slight over-use of sequencing · few minor errors.

samples.text:
The charts illustrate how the populations of two countries were distributed across five age groups in 2020.

The two countries display almost opposite demographic profiles: Country A's population was heavily weighted towards the young, whereas Country B's was concentrated in the older age brackets.

In Country A, the proportion of the population fell consistently with each successive age group. Children under 15 constituted the largest segment, at 41%, and when the 15–29 group (28%) is added, it becomes clear that over two-thirds of the population were under 30. The share then tapered to 16% for those aged 30–44 and 11% for the 45–64 age group, and people aged 65 and over made up a mere 4%.

Country B, by contrast, had a markedly older population. The largest group was aged 45–64, at 28%, and the over-65s accounted for almost a quarter (24%), a proportion six times higher than in Country A. Those aged 30–44 represented 19%, while the younger groups were comparatively small: 16% were aged 15–29 and only 13% were children, less than a third of the equivalent figure for Country A. In other words, more than half of Country B's population was 45 or older.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected and compared · clear overview framing the contrast · accurate derived comparisons · cohesion managed naturally · precise vocabulary (tapered, weighted towards) · wide, accurate range of structures.
